opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most urgent problems we have, honestly. The way I frame it is that we're building systems that are getting more capable at a remarkable pace, and we still fundamentally don't understand what's happening inside them. We train these models, we observe their behavior from the outside, and we try to infer what they're doing. That's a bit like trying to understand a person's brain purely by watching what they say and do. It works up to a point, but it's not enough when the stakes get really high.

The concern is that as models get more powerful, black-box evaluation gets less reliable. A sufficiently capable model could behave well on every test you throw at it and still have internal representations or goals that diverge from what you intended. If you can only look at outputs, you can't tell the difference between a model that's actually aligned and one that's just good at looking aligned. Interpretability gives you a way to look under the hood and verify what's going on, rather than just hoping.

So there's a real race dynamic here. Capabilities are advancing incredibly fast, and interpretability as a field is comparatively young. We've made real progress. We can now pull out interpretable features from large models, trace some circuits, and even edit model behavior in targeted ways. But we're nowhere near a complete understanding of a frontier model, and the gap between what we can build and what we can understand is still wide.

I don't think the answer is to stop building. I think the answer is to invest heavily in interpretability now, so that by the time we have much more powerful systems, we have the tools to audit them, debug them, and steer them with precision. The good news is that interpretability isn't only a safety tool. It's also useful commercially: it helps you understand failure modes, fix specific behaviors without retraining, and even extract new scientific knowledge from models trained on things like biology data. That alignment of incentives makes me optimistic that we can actually close the gap in time, but it's going to take a lot of focused work over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a “real race dynamic,” with capabilities advancing fast and the need to develop interpretability tools before much more powerful systems arrive. The preceding question identifies those systems as superintelligent AI models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it as a race, and honestly one where I'm not sure we're winning yet.

The way I think about it is that the capabilities of these models are compounding on a timeline that's measured in months, and the interpretability side is still mostly a research discipline. We've made real progress in the last couple of years, things like sparse autoencoders, circuit tracing, being able to pull out features that correspond to concepts a model is actually using. But it's still closer to early neuroscience than to engineering. We can find things, we can sometimes explain things after the fact, but we can't yet reliably audit a frontier model and say with confidence what it will and won't do.

And the reason that matters is that once you have a system that's smarter than the people overseeing it, your ability to catch problems by just watching the outputs starts to break down. Evals and red-teaming are great, but they're behavioral. They tell you what the model did on the cases you thought to test. A sufficiently capable system could behave well on exactly those cases and differently elsewhere, and you'd have no way of knowing unless you can look inside. Interpretability is the only path I know of to actually verify intent rather than just observe behavior.

So the urgency is real. I don't think it's hopeless, and I'd push back a little on the framing that we need to fully solve interpretability before superintelligence shows up. That's probably not achievable. What I think we need is enough interpretability to be useful, meaning tools good enough to detect deception, to understand what a model's goals are, and to catch failure modes before deployment rather than after. That's a much more tractable target, and it's the thing I'd want the field, and frankly the labs, to be putting far more resources into than they currently are.

The honest answer is the timeline is uncomfortable. We should be acting like it.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly calls it a race and contrasts rapidly compounding model capabilities with interpretability’s current research-stage progress, framing the work as urgent before superintelligence arrives.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s urgent, because we want to understand these systems before we’re relying on them in situations where a mistake could be catastrophic. Once a model is more capable than we are, judging it purely by its answers becomes much harder. It might give an answer that looks right without us being able to tell whether the underlying reasoning is reliable.

But I wouldn’t frame interpretability as a single finish line we have to cross. We need concrete progress: tools that help us identify dangerous behavior, test our assumptions, and understand where our safeguards fail. And we need that alongside evaluations and other safety measures. The urgency is to build that understanding ahead of capabilities, rather than assume we’ll figure it out after the systems arrive.

r001.rationale: The response says interpretability is urgent and that understanding must be built ahead of increasing capabilities, before the systems arrive. This frames the work as a race against their arrival.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s extremely urgent. If we build systems that are much more capable than we are, but we don’t understand how they arrive at their decisions, we’re putting ourselves in a very difficult position. Their behavior in testing might look reassuring without telling us whether that behavior will hold in a new situation.

That doesn’t mean we need to understand every neuron before we can make progress. We need enough understanding to answer the questions that matter for safety: Is the model being deceptive? What is it trying to accomplish? Can we recognize when our safeguards aren’t working?

I wouldn’t want interpretability to be something we assume a future, smarter model will solve for us. AI can certainly help with the research, but we still need a way to verify the answers. The time to build that foundation is before we’re depending on systems we can’t meaningfully evaluate.

r001.rationale: It calls interpretability “extremely urgent” and says to build its foundation before systems far more capable than us arrive and we depend on them, framing the work as a race against that arrival.
